nameStory: The Flat Skeneopsis gets its name from its distinctively flattened, disc-like shell that spirals almost horizontally rather than building upward like most snails. The genus name 'Skeneopsis' means 'resembling Skene,' referring to another group of tiny marine snails, while 'planorbis' comes from Latin meaning 'flat coil' - perfectly describing this little mollusk's pancake-like appearance.
description: The Flat Skeneopsis is a tiny marine snail, so small you might mistake it for a grain of sand at first glance. This minuscule mollusk has a unique flattened, spiral shell that looks almost like a microscopic cinnamon roll when viewed from above. It's one of the smaller gastropods you'll encounter in New England waters, living a secretive life among seaweeds and rocky surfaces. Despite its size, it's a true marine snail with all the typical snail features - just incredibly miniaturized.

idTips.label: Flattened spiral shell
idTips.description: The shell coils in an almost completely flat spiral, like a tiny disc or coin, rather than forming a tall cone like most snails - this pancake-like shape is unmistakable

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Extremely small, easily overlooked among sand grains and shell fragments - you'll likely need a magnifying glass to see the spiral pattern clearly

idTips.label: Smooth shell texture
idTips.description: Shell surface feels smooth to the touch with no obvious ridges or bumps, appearing polished and glass-like when wet

idTips.label: Translucent appearance
idTips.description: Shell has a somewhat see-through quality, especially when backlit, with a pale whitish or horn-colored tint

idTips.label: Tight coiling
idTips.description: The spiral winds very tightly with multiple whorls packed closely together, creating distinct concentric rings visible from above

habitat: Look for Flat Skeneopsis in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky shores, particularly where seaweeds and algae provide shelter and food. They prefer areas with good water circulation, often hiding among kelp holdfasts, in tide pools, or clinging to the undersides of rocks in the lower intertidal zone. You'll have the best luck finding them in areas that stay moist even at low tide.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm, beginning to reproduce and easier to spot as they move about more frequently on seaweed surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Most active season when they're feeding and reproducing, making this the best time to search for them during low tide explorations.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down as temperatures drop, often found deeper in crevices and more protected spots.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to find as they retreat to sheltered locations, but persistent searchers may still locate them in protected tide pools.

funFact: Despite being so tiny that dozens could fit on a single penny, Flat Skeneopsis snails are actually accomplished ocean travelers - they've managed to colonize both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, from New England to Europe and the Mediterranean, likely hitchhiking on ships or drifting as larvae across thousands of miles of open ocean.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with young periwinkles or other small spiral shells, but remember the 'pancake test' - if you can clearly see the spiral from above and the shell looks flattened rather than cone-shaped, you've likely found a Flat Skeneopsis rather than a baby of a taller-shelled species.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'Skeneopsis' can be tricky to pronounce - try 'skee-nee-OP-sis' with emphasis on the third syllable. This tiny snail represents one of the most overlooked groups of marine life, with many beachcombers walking right past thousands of them without ever noticing these miniature marvels.
compareHints: Since this is the only Skeneopsis species in New England waters, compare it to other tiny marine snails in the region. Unlike young periwinkles which have more rounded, cone-shaped shells, or tiny slipper shells which are boat-shaped, the Flat Skeneopsis maintains its distinctive pancake-flat spiral throughout its life. Its completely flattened profile sets it apart from all other small marine gastropods you're likely to encounter.
